rhythm.value: Detector: 14 shots, median 1.1 s. Corrected: the film has three speeds. 0-2.1 s is one slow shot. 2.1-2.9 s is eight hard cuts at 2-4 frames (0.1 s median). 2.9-6.9 s is one continuous move of 4 s. Stats hold one line of text for 6.17 s over background cuts, quick at first (every 2-3 frames to 7.4 s), then 30-60 frames apart. The end is four word-shots of 0.9-1.6 s. Sound was not heard. No speech was detected. Tempo reads 128.38 BPM with confidence only 0.456 (beatRegularity 0.96), so treat it as doubtful. Level jumps at about 4.2 s (section 1 energy 0.21, section 2 energy 0.50). audio.json onsets are too dense to show structure, so I measured 50 ms RMS peaks from the media: 4.0, 4.7, 5.6, 7.0, 7.7, 8.45, 9.35, (10.05), 10.75, 11.45, 12.1, 13.05, 14.45, 15.15, 15.85, 16.75. That is one uneven figure repeating about every 3.7 s (+0, +0.7, +1.6, +3.0 s; 10.05 is an extra), which is 8 beats at the measured tempo, so the tempo may be right despite its low confidence. Four of the five main picture changes fall within 0.1 s of a swell: 6.9 (7.0), 11.4 (11.45), 13.07 (13.05), 15.07 (15.15); 16.17 does not. With 16 peaks in 13.5 s, a random time lands within 0.1 s about 24% of the time. I chose those five main changes after seeing the peaks, so this is suggestive rather than proved. What makes the swells cannot be told without hearing. cutsOnBeat 0.462 vs chance 0.338: weak. cutsOnOnset 0.923 vs chance 0.706, on 13 cuts: suggestive only, because onsets are dense. The 0.1 s page cuts cannot each be on an onset, so they are not cut to sound one by one.
evidence: 50 ms RMS peaks of media/source.mp4, computed for this analysis, not in a measured layer

value.name: highlight-locked-smash-cut
value.description: Highlight-locked smash cut. Eight different pages (F63, F67, F69, F72, F75, F78, F82, F84) held 2-4 frames each. In each, a yellow highlight on the same phrase sits within a few percent of frame centre. Page scale changes, but the marked phrase stays the same size to the eye, so it reads as a single object with worlds changing round it.
value.why: A human eye settles on the stable bright point, so a run this fast still reads. The film saves cost as well: the pages need only be credible for 3 frames.

value.name: one-becomes-crowd-pull-out
value.description: From lips to a crowd in one move. Card begins as a crop of lips (F87) and opens to a person in 6 frames. The column scrolls with a soft white halo at each card's edge. At 4.5 s, white blurred tiles appear left and right, resolving to video outward from the centre by F148. The wall continues to shrink, from about 6 to about 16 columns, until 6.9 s.
value.why: The move turns one person into a statistic physically. The white blank tiles look like content loading, which supports the idea that there's more and more.

value.name: caption-anchor-over-footage-stutter
value.description: A centred sentence over dim hard cuts. The line keeps one height and stays centred as it builds: each new word arrives yellow and cools to white in about 9 frames, and earlier words slide left to make room. A yellow pill opens empty (F215-F216) and fills with its words (F217), and later jumps to the figure (F309). A source line types itself at the bottom. Footage at about 25% brightness cuts every 2-3 frames to 7.4 s, then every 30-60 frames. One grey frame at F219. Words delete in groups to end a sentence, and those left do not move, so gaps stay open (F264, F339).
value.why: The picture keeps changing while the eye stays on one short line, so the film can hold a reading pace while its energy stays up.

value.name: lens-pass-word-track
value.description: Size as emphasis, words as a passing camera. 'What' enters at the right edge, soft and bluish, focuses as it nears the centre (F396), 'if' follows, and both drift out soft at the left. Then 'there was a', tiny and nearly still, in black for 0.8 s. Hard cut to 'better' at 83% of width, blue, with a bloom. Hard cut to 'way?', with light rising from the corner. File ends mid-motion.
value.why: The smallest words get the longest pause, so the viewer waits; then the biggest word arrives.
